items.title: Latent demand is real in general practice
items.body: The idea that cheaper intelligence unlocks demand has a clear NHS parallel: faster, cheaper access has historically increased contacts rather than reduced them. If AI makes advice, summaries and follow-up cheap, expect more questions and more patient-held information arriving in the surgery, not fewer. Planning on the basis that AI simply saves time is optimistic.

items.title: Who shares the surplus?
items.body: Rao's point that the politics shifts to fair access to cognitive abundance matters for the NHS. Scribes and triage tools may free clinician minutes, but whether that time goes back to patients, to extra list demand, or to cost-cutting is a commissioning decision, not a technical one. Worth watching how ICB contracts treat any time saved.

items.title: Little direct clinical relevance
items.body: This edition is a philosophical essay, and there is no direct guidance for the consulting room. The sceptical counterweight is that demand growth and abundance claims are untested, and transition costs, which NLW concedes, fall on real staff.
